findings.title: Validator has a write side effect and runs on every validation
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? increments match_count and saves the record on every call. Because the validator runs on any `valid?` call, one signup can be counted several times. In UsersController#create, `user.valid?` runs and then `user.save` validates again, so each attempt increments the count twice. The statistics are therefore inflated, and a validation step writes to the database even if the surrounding transaction is later rolled back.

findings.title: Case-sensitive email lookup lets blocks be bypassed
findings.body: BlockedEmail.where(email: email) is an exact, case-sensitive match. Email is neither downcased nor normalized when stored or looked up. A blocked address such as bad@spam.com is bypassed by Bad@Spam.com. The same normalization gap affects the uniqueness validation.

findings.title: Racy read-modify-write on match_count
findings.body: match_count += 1 followed by save is a read-modify-write on the Ruby side. Concurrent signups for the same email can lose updates. An atomic `increment_counter` or an SQL `UPDATE ... SET match_count = match_count + 1` avoids this.

findings.title: Shared array literal in controller prototype
findings.body: `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is declared on the class prototype. The same array instance is therefore shared by all instances of the controller, and `pushObject` mutates it. Rejected emails persist across instances. It should be initialized in `init`.

findings.title: Every email error marks the email as rejected
findings.body: Any server-side email error, such as 'already taken', is treated as a rejected email. The client then shows the generic 'invalid' message instead of the server's reason. A transient error would also permanently reject that address in the client.
